title: Opinions and disagreement
cando: agree and disagree politely, and give your reasons

about.text: In this lesson you give your opinion, and you agree and disagree politely at a residents' meeting. You read the minutes of the meeting and a complaint letter that nobody answered. Then you write a better letter, with four clear points.
goals: Disagree politely: I see your point, but … I'm not sure I agree.
Join different ideas with although, however and while.
Make what you say softer with may, might and could.
Read meeting minutes, and write a letter with four clear points.
Disagree with a proposal at a meeting, and suggest another one.

chapters.title: A residents' meeting
chapters.text:
In this lesson, you disagree politely, and you give your reasons.
First, you listen to a residents' meeting in a block of flats called Priory Court. The residents are deciding how to spend some money.
The chair, Grace, proposes cameras at the front entrance. Not everyone agrees.
Listen to how people disagree without being rude. Omar says: I see your point, but is that really our biggest issue? Lena says: I'm not sure I agree. And Grace answers: That's true. However, two bikes were stolen.
Notice that nobody says: You're wrong. First, they show that they understand. Then they give a different view, and a reason.

chapters.title: Joining ideas, and sounding softer
chapters.text:
There are two grammar points in this lesson.
The first is how to join two different ideas. Although joins them in one sentence: Although the cameras are useful, they are expensive. However starts a new sentence: The cameras are useful. However, they are expensive. Put a full stop before however, and a comma after it. While compares two things: While Lena wants a lock, Grace wants cameras.
The second point is how to make what you say softer. Use may, might and could. They might cost more than we think. That may not be the best idea. We could put a light on the bike store.
These small words make you sound polite, and people listen to you more.

chapters.title: Minutes and a letter
chapters.text:
Next, you read two documents.
The first is the minutes of the meeting. Minutes are a short written record of what people said and decided.
The second is a letter that a resident sent to the council. Nobody replied to it. Read it, and think about why. Look at the tone. Is it polite? Is it clear what he wants?
Then you write a better letter. Say what you want at the start. Give four clear points: firstly, secondly, thirdly and lastly. And keep the tone polite.

chapters.title: Disagree and suggest
chapters.text:
Then you go to a residents' meeting yourself. The chair proposes a new rule, and you don't agree with it.
First, show that you understand: I see your point. Then give your reason. Then suggest a different idea: We could do this instead.
For example: I see your point, but many people get home late from work. We could keep the garden open until ten, and ask people to be quiet after nine.
Stay calm and polite. You might not win the vote, but people will respect you.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Finally, you read a story or an article about people who disagree.
Read it once for the main story. Then read it again and answer the questions.
Think about each person's point of view. Who do you agree with, and why?

warmup.prompt: Your neighbours want to change something in your building, and you don't agree. What do you do?
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. Many people say nothing, because they don't want an argument. In this lesson you learn to disagree in a polite way, so that people listen to you.

conversation.title: At the residents' meeting
conversation.setting: The residents of Priory Court, a block of council flats, meet once a month. Tonight they are deciding how to spend the residents' fund. Grace is the chair.
lines: Right, the next item on the agenda is the residents' fund. We have £3,000 this year, and I'd like to propose that we spend it on cameras at the front entrance.
I see your point, but is that really our biggest issue? As far as I know, nobody has broken in this year.
That's true. However, two bikes were stolen from the bike store last month.
I'm not sure I agree with the cameras. They might cost more than we think, and some people may not want to be filmed.
Fair enough. So what would you suggest, Lena?
We could put a stronger lock and a light on the bike store. That would be much cheaper.
Can I raise another concern? Three flats on the ground floor have damp, and the heating keeps breaking down.
You have a point, Omar, although repairs are the council's job. We can't pay for them from the fund.
I know. But I've written to the council twice, and nobody has replied. Maybe we could write again, all together this time.
I'm strongly in favour of that. A letter from the whole building might convince them.
OK, let's vote. Who's in favour of the cameras? … Four. And the lock, the light and a letter to the council? … Eleven.
While I respect your point of view, I still think we need cameras. But let's agree to disagree.
Thank you, Kwame. So, the lock, the light and the letter. Omar, will you help me write it?
Of course. Let's keep the tone polite this time.

questions.q: What does Grace propose at the start?
questions.a: spending the fund on cameras at the front entrance
questions.why: Grace says: I'd like to propose that we spend it on cameras at the front entrance.

questions.a: a stronger lock and a light on the bike store
questions.why: Lena says: We could put a stronger lock and a light on the bike store.

questions.q: Why can't the residents pay for the damp and heating repairs from the fund?
wrong: Nobody has damp in their flat.
questions.why: Grace says: repairs are the council's job. We can't pay for them from the fund.

phrases.use: Showing that you understand someone, before you disagree.
Agreeing with one part, then adding a different point.
Saying that someone's idea is partly right.
Accepting what someone says, even if you don't agree with all of it.
Ending a disagreement in a friendly way.

items.meaning: A person's opinion, or their way of looking at something.
items.example: I understand your point of view, but I don't agree.

items.meaning: If someone has a point, what they say is partly true or sensible.
items.example: You have a point. The cameras would be expensive.

items.meaning: You say this when you accept what someone says, even if you don't completely agree.
items.example: “I can't come on Monday.” “Fair enough. What about Tuesday?”

items.meaning: To accept that two people have different opinions, and stop arguing about it.
items.example: We'll never agree about this, so let's agree to disagree.

items.meaning: To suggest a plan or an idea for other people to think about, especially at a meeting.
items.example: I propose that we meet once a month.

items.meaning: Supporting a plan or an idea.
items.example: Most residents are in favour of the new rules.

items.meaning: To say that you are against something, or that you don't like it.
items.example: Several neighbours objected to the noise from the new bar.

items.meaning: To choose between plans or people, for example by raising your hand or by writing on a paper.
items.example: We voted to paint the entrance hall.

items.meaning: A worry about something.
items.example: My main concern is safety on the stairs.

items.meaning: A problem or a subject that people talk about or need to deal with.
items.example: Parking is a big issue in our street.

items.meaning: To start talking about a subject or a problem, for example at a meeting.
items.example: Can I raise one more issue before we finish?

items.meaning: The group of people who run a town or an area. They look after things like roads, rubbish collection and some of the housing.
items.example: Our block of flats belongs to the council.

items.meaning: To make someone believe that something is true or right.
items.example: She convinced me that the plan would work.

items.meaning: To accept someone's opinions or feelings, even when you don't share them.
items.example: I respect your view, but I don't share it.

items.meaning: Very much, and with strong feelings.
items.example: I feel strongly about this, so I'm going to speak at the meeting.

sound.title: The weak first sound: agree, concern, propose
sound.explain: Many words in this lesson have a weak first part and a strong second part. The first part is short and quiet, like the a in about: a-GREE, con-CERN, pro-POSE. Don't make the first part strong. Listen, then say each group.
lines: I'd like to propose another idea.

sayIt.instructions: Say Omar's and Lena's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Do you sound calm and polite, not angry?
lines: I see your point, but is that really our biggest issue? As far as I know, nobody has broken in this year.
I'm not sure I agree with the cameras. They might cost more than we think, and some people may not want to be filmed.
We could put a stronger lock and a light on the bike store. That would be much cheaper.
Can I raise another concern? Three flats on the ground floor have damp, and the heating keeps breaking down.

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the meeting.
examples: That's true. However, two bikes were stolen.
You have a point, Omar, although repairs are the council's job.
They might cost more than we think.
We could put a stronger lock on the bike store.
spot.question: Which sentences join two different ideas? Where is however, and where is although? Which words make the speakers sound softer and more polite?
spot.answer: However starts a new sentence, after a full stop, with a comma after it. Although joins two ideas inside one sentence. Might and could make the speakers softer: They might cost more is less strong than They will cost more, and We could … is a polite suggestion.

rules.title: although, however, while
rule: although + a clause, in the same sentence: Although the cameras are useful, they're expensive.
although can also go in the middle: I agree, although it will take time.
however starts a new sentence: The cameras are useful. However, they're expensive.
Put a full stop before however, and a comma after it.
while compares two things: While Lena wants a lock, Kwame wants cameras.
rules.mistake: Not: It's useful, however it's expensive. Say: It's useful. However, it's expensive.

rules.title: may, might, could to soften what you say
rule: may / might + a verb when you are not sure: It might cost more. People may not like it.
could for a polite suggestion: We could put a light on the bike store.
Softer: That might not be the best idea. Stronger: That's a bad idea.
Polite openings: I may be wrong, but … It might be better to …
No to and no s after may, might and could: It might cost more.
rules.mistake: Not: It might costs more. Not: It might to cost more. Say: It might cost more.

practice.q: The cameras are useful. ___ , they're very expensive.
practice.why: However starts a new sentence, with a comma after it.

practice.q: ___ the lift is old, it still works well.
practice.why: Although + a clause joins two different ideas in one sentence.

practice.q: I agree with you, ___ it will take time.
practice.why: Although can join two ideas in the middle of a sentence. However can't join them with a comma.

practice.q: ___ some residents want cameras, others want a better lock.
practice.why: While compares two different ideas in one sentence.

options: The flat is big. However, it's very cold.
The flat is big, however it's very cold.
The flat is big however, it's very cold.
practice.a: The flat is big. However, it's very cold.
practice.why: However starts a new sentence, and a comma goes after it.

practice.q: The new plan ___ cost more than we think.
practice.why: Might + a verb, with no to and no s.

practice.q: Which is the most polite way to disagree?
options: That might not be the best idea.
practice.a: That might not be the best idea.
practice.why: Might makes the disagreement softer and more polite.

practice.q: A polite suggestion: We ___ ask the council for help.
practice.why: Could + a verb, with no to, makes a soft suggestion.

practice.q: I ___ be wrong, but I think the lift is more important.
practice.why: I may be wrong, but … makes your opinion softer.

practice.q: The cameras ___ help, but I'm not sure.
practice.why: Might shows that you are not sure.

yourTurn.prompt: Your neighbour says: “I think we should close the garden at night. People make too much noise there.” Disagree politely. Say what is true, give your reason, and suggest another idea. Use although or however, and may, might or could.
yourTurn.model: You have a point. The noise can be a problem. However, a lot of people use the garden after work, and closing it might upset them. Although it's noisy sometimes, it's usually quiet after ten. We could put up a sign and ask people to be quiet after nine.

text.title: The minutes, and a letter nobody answered
text.type: Meeting minutes and a complaint letter
text.body:
PRIORY COURT RESIDENTS' GROUP
Minutes of the meeting on Tuesday 4 March, 7 p.m., in the community room
Present: 15 residents. Chair: Grace Mensah

1. Residents' fund (£3,000)
Grace proposed cameras at the front entrance. She pointed out that two bikes were stolen from the bike store in February. Lena proposed a stronger lock and a light for the bike store. Residents voted: 4 for the cameras, 11 for the lock and the light. Lena will get two prices by 1 April.

2. Damp and heating
Omar raised the matter of damp in flats 1, 3 and 5. The heating has broken down repeatedly since November. Omar wrote to the council in December and January, but nobody replied. The matter remains open. Grace and Omar will write a new letter from the whole group, with a polite tone and four clear points. It will ask the council to take action by 30 April.

3. Any other business: none.
Next meeting: Tuesday 1 April, 7 p.m. Please send items for the agenda to Grace by 25 March.

- - - - - - - -

Flat 3, Priory Court
10 January

To the council,
This is the second time I am writing, and I am very angry. The heating in this building is terrible. It has broken down again and again, and it is always cold. My bathroom is full of damp, and it smells. My neighbours have the same problem. I phoned your office repeatedly, but nobody ever called me back. The lift was broken last month too, and the lights on the stairs don't work. Your staff are useless. I pay my rent every month, so why don't you do your job?

Omar Haddad

gist.q: Which problem is in both documents?
gist.a: the damp and the heating in the flats
gist.why: The minutes and Omar's letter both talk about the damp and the heating.
The minutes say: Omar wrote to the council in December and January, but nobody replied.

detail.q: How did the residents vote on the fund?
detail.a: 4 for the cameras, 11 for the lock and the light
wrong: 11 for the cameras, 4 for the lock and the light
detail.why: The minutes say: Residents voted: 4 for the cameras, 11 for the lock and the light.

detail.q: What will Grace and Omar do about the damp and the heating?
detail.a: write a new letter from the whole group
wrong: pay for the repairs from the fund
detail.why: The minutes say: Grace and Omar will write a new letter from the whole group.

detail.q: What is wrong with the tone of Omar's letter?
detail.why: He writes that he is very angry, and that the staff are useless.

detail.q: What is missing from Omar's letter?
detail.a: what he wants the council to do, and by when
wrong: his name and his flat number
detail.why: He lists a lot of problems, but he never says what he wants the council to do, or by when.

items.meaning: The written record of what people said and decided at a meeting.
items.example: The minutes of the last meeting are on the noticeboard.

items.meaning: A list of the things that people will talk about at a meeting.
items.example: Is the car park on the agenda this month?

items.meaning: A subject or a situation that you need to think about or deal with.
items.example: The heating is an urgent matter.

items.meaning: To stay the same, or to stay in the same place or situation.
items.example: Two repairs remain unfinished.

items.meaning: Water in the walls or the air of a building. It makes rooms smell, and it can make people ill.
items.example: There's damp on the bathroom wall again.

items.meaning: The system that keeps a building warm, for example the radiators and the boiler.
items.example: The heating isn't working again.

items.meaning: The feeling in the way someone writes or speaks, for example polite, friendly or angry.
items.example: Keep the tone of your letter polite.

items.meaning: To do something to solve a problem.
items.example: The council must take action before the winter.

items.meaning: To tell someone a fact that they did not know or had not thought about.
items.example: She pointed out that the lift had broken three times.

items.meaning: Many times, again and again.
items.example: I've asked repeatedly for a new lock.

model.title: A letter with four clear points
model.body:
Dear Ms Adeyemi,

Damp and heating, Priory Court

I am writing for the Priory Court Residents' Group about repairs that remain unfinished. We would like a date for each repair by 30 April.

Firstly, three flats on the ground floor (1, 3 and 5) have had damp since October.
Secondly, the heating has broken down five times since November.
Thirdly, residents wrote to you in December and in January, but we have not had a reply.
Lastly, two of our residents are over eighty, and a cold, damp flat may be dangerous for their health.

We understand that you are very busy. However, we hope that you will take action before next winter.

Yours sincerely,
Grace Mensah
Chair, Priory Court Residents' Group

write.task: Write a letter about a problem where you live or work. Say what you want at the start. Then give four clear points, and end politely. Use however or although once, and may, might or could once. It can be real or made up.
checklist: I said what I want, and by when, at the start.
I wrote four clear points: firstly, secondly, thirdly, lastly.
My tone is polite: there are no angry or rude words.
I used however or although, and may, might or could.

card.title: Disagree and suggest
card.situation: You are at a residents' meeting in your block of flats. The chair proposes to close the shared garden at 8 p.m. every evening, because of noise. Some people agree, but you don't.
card.goal: Say politely that you disagree, and give your reasons. Then suggest a different idea, and try to convince the others to vote for it.

phrases: I'm not sure I agree. Many people use the garden after work.
prepare.notes: Write down two reasons, and your own idea. Think about what the others might say, and how you will answer them politely.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, your teacher is the chair and proposes to close the garden at 8 p.m. Disagree politely, give two reasons and suggest another idea. At the end, the class votes.
doIt.wehel: You are the chair of a residents' meeting in a block of flats. Propose to close the shared garden at 8 p.m. because of noise. I will disagree politely and suggest another idea. Give me reasons for your proposal, and ask me questions. If my reasons are good, agree to a vote. Use simple English.

model.title: At the meeting
lines: The next item is the garden. Some residents have complained about noise, so I propose that we close it at 8 p.m.
I see your point, but I'm not sure I agree. Many people only get home from work at six or seven.
That's true. However, the noise is a real issue for the ground-floor flats.
You have a point. But closing at eight might be unfair to everyone, because of a few noisy people.
We could keep it open until ten, and ask people to be quiet after nine. We could put up a sign, too.
I'm in favour of that. It would be fair for everyone.
Then we could raise it again at the next meeting.
Fair enough. Let's vote. Who's in favour of the new idea?
compare: Did you show that you understood the proposal before you disagreed?
Did you suggest another idea with could or might?
Did you stay calm and polite?

canDo: I can agree and disagree politely: I see your point, but …
I can join different ideas with although, however and while.
I can make what I say softer with may, might and could.
I can read meeting minutes, and write a letter with four clear points.
I can disagree with a proposal at a meeting, and suggest another one.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first page. Who do you think disagrees in this story, and what about?
reading.talk: Who was right in the story, in your opinion? Do you agree with the ending? Write three or four sentences with although or however, or discuss it with Wehel.

quiz.q: It's a good idea. ___ , it's too expensive.
quiz.why: However starts a new sentence, with a comma after it.

quiz.q: ___ the flat is small, it's very comfortable.
quiz.why: Although + a clause joins two different ideas in one sentence.

quiz.q: Which is the most polite way to disagree?
options: I see your point, but I'm not sure I agree.
quiz.a: I see your point, but I'm not sure I agree.
quiz.why: You show that you understand first, then you disagree softly.

quiz.q: The repairs ___ take a few weeks.
quiz.why: Might + a verb, with no to and no s.

quiz.q: Raise your hand if you want to ___ for the new lock.
quiz.why: When you vote, you choose, for example by raising your hand.

quiz.q: The written record of a meeting is called the ___ .
quiz.why: The minutes say what people said and decided.

quiz.q: I'm strongly in favour ___ the new lock.
quiz.why: In favour of + a noun: in favour of the new lock.

quiz.q: The heating ___ last week, but it has broken down again.
quiz.why: The passive in the past: was + past participle.

quiz.q: 'The lift is broken again.' → He said that the lift ___ broken again.
quiz.why: In reported speech, is often moves back to was.

quiz.q: This winter the heating broke down ___ times as last winter: six, not three.
quiz.why: Six is two times three: twice as many.

liveClass: Day 1: practise the residents' meeting in groups of four. Then change the proposal: a new car park, no barbecues in the garden, a higher service charge.
Day 2: soften it. Say a strong sentence (That's wrong. We must do it now.), and the learners make it polite with may, might, could, although or however.
Day 3: the task. You chair a residents' meeting and propose to close the garden at 8 p.m. Each learner disagrees politely and suggests another idea. The class votes at the end.
Day 4: talk about the book and answer questions. Then learners read their four-point letters aloud, and the class checks the tone and the four points.
